name: Angola
summary: A country on the Atlantic coast of southern Africa, a Portuguese colony for centuries, independent in 1975 and then torn by civil war until 2002.

knownFor.label: Queen Nzinga
knownFor.note: A 17th-century ruler who resisted the Portuguese, now a national heroine.

terrain.value: Coastal plain, central plateau, Namib desert in the south.

climate.value: Tropical on the coast and in the north with a rainy season; drier in the south and the Namib desert strip.

resources.value: Oil and diamonds, plus iron ore, farmland, coffee and fish.

disasters.value: Droughts in the south and floods in the north; landmines left by the war still harm farmers.

urbanisation.value: Luanda is one of Africa’s largest cities.

disease.value: Malaria; landmines and minefields remain from the war.

migration.value: Millions were displaced during the civil war (1975–2002), and many Portuguese settlers left at independence.

economicBase.value: Oil (an OPEC member; about 1.165 million barrels a day in 2022).

tradeRoutes.value: Oil exports by sea, mainly to China, India and Europe, through terminals off Cabinda and Luanda.

wealth.value: Oil made the country rich on paper, but the wealth is unevenly shared and most people remain poor.

moneyAndTax.value: The kwanza, introduced in 1977 and reissued several times; government income depends heavily on oil taxes.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic; the MPLA ran a one-party state from 1975 to 1991.

keyRulers.value: Agostinho Neto (MPLA chairman). José Eduardo dos Santos (led the country for 38 years, until 2017). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: The MPLA party has governed since independence, and the president is chosen through elections within a dominant-party system.

institutions.value: A strong presidency, a National Assembly, and a legal system based on Portuguese law.

stability.value: A civil war lasted from 1975 to 2002; since the peace the country has been stable but with limited political openness.

eliteConflict.value: The MPLA and UNITA fought for control of the state from 1975 to 2002, with the FNLA as a third movement at the start.

armyAndTech.value: The USSR and Cuba backed the MPLA; the US and South Africa backed UNITA.

majorWars.value: The Angolan Civil War (1975–2002), which drew in Cuba, South Africa, the Soviet Union and the United States.

territoryChange.value: The borders drawn in the colonial period have stayed the same since independence, including the Cabinda exclave.

alliancesRivals.value: Close ties with Portugal and China; Cuba and the Soviet Union backed the MPLA, South Africa and the United States backed UNITA during the war.

inventions.value: No major inventions; Angolan craft traditions and music are the best-known cultural exports.

scienceEducation.value: Schools and universities were rebuilt after the war; literacy has risen but quality varies.

openness.value: Open to foreign investors and trade, but closed in politics for much of the post-war period.

communicationTransport.value: The Benguela Railway, from the coast to the Congo and Zambia border, was destroyed in the war and rebuilt by 2015.

languageWriting.value: Portuguese is official; Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo are the most widely spoken indigenous languages.

artsArchitecture.value: Semba and kizomba music, carved masks and figures such as Chokwe sculpture, and Portuguese colonial buildings.

socialStructure.value: A small, rich elite and a large poor majority; many Angolans live in cities such as Luanda.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared national identity grew after the independence struggle and the war, alongside Ovimbundu, Mbundu and Bakongo ethnic ties.

dailyLife.value: City apartments and musseques (informal settlements); funge, fish, beans.

neighbours.value: The Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo (Cabinda), Zambia and Namibia.

ideasReligions.value: Marxism-Leninism was the state ideology in the 1970s–80s; Christianity (mostly Catholic) is now the main religion.

colonisation.value: Portuguese colony from the 16th century until 1975.

riseSignals.value: Independence from Portugal on 11 November 1975, after the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon.

peakPeriod.value: Growth after the 2002 peace settlement, driven largely by oil revenue.

declineSignals.value: The 2014 oil price collapse led to IMF support and fiscal consolidation.

outcome.value: Angola continues as an independent state, with peace since 2002.
